transcript.text: Thanks, Elena. To your question about risks in moving to dismiss -- I see a few intersections we need to think through carefully. First, on the merits of the motion itself, my analysis is that five of seven directors were independent at the time of demand, which under controlling precedent should defeat the demand-futility allegations. That's a strong procedural basis for a motion to dismiss, and it would avoid the complications that come with a negotiated resolution -- specifically, Victor's carrier consent requirements for any admission or settlement and Maya's constraint that any negotiated resolution be limited to governance reforms only with no monetary payment and no admission. So in some respects, moving to dismiss sidesteps several of the constraints the group has flagged. However, I'd flag two things for the group's consideration. First, Nadia's special committee requirement is triggered if any resolution contains a governance undertaking -- if we file a motion to dismiss without any governance commitments, that requirement may not be implicated, but we should confirm that with Nadia. Second, Victor's 10-business-day notice requirement applies regardless of which path we take -- even a motion to dismiss is a 'response' that likely triggers the carrier notice obligation, so we need to ensure notice is given within that window no matter what. I don't see a direct conflict between moving to dismiss and the other constraints, but I'd want Victor to confirm whether the carrier's notice clock has already started or starts when we file, and I'd want Nadia to confirm whether a motion to dismiss alone -- with no governance undertakings -- avoids the special committee requirement. If both of those check out, I'd recommend we authorize a motion to dismiss as the primary strategy, with notice to the carrier immediately.

transcript.text: Thanks, Nadia. Thomas, to your question about the carrier's notice clock -- I want to be clear on the timeline. The 10-business-day notice requirement runs from the date we become aware of the claim, which in this case is the date the derivative complaint was served on the company. I've confirmed this from the D&O policy language in my coverage file. So the clock has already started, and we need to ensure notice is given to the carrier within that window regardless of whether we file a motion to dismiss or pursue any other path. I'd recommend we authorize notice to the carrier today or tomorrow at the latest to make sure we're within the 10-business-day window. I do not see any conflict between the motion to dismiss strategy and the carrier's notice requirements -- notice can be given independent of whatever response we ultimately file, and since a motion to dismiss would not involve any admission or settlement, the carrier's written consent requirement for admissions and settlements would not be triggered. That said, I want to flag for the group that if we later pivot from a motion to dismiss to any negotiated resolution, the carrier's written consent requirement would kick in before we could make any admission or enter any settlement -- and given Maya's constraint that the board has authorized governance reforms only with no admission and no monetary payment, that should be manageable, but we'd need to build in time for carrier review. My recommendation is: authorize carrier notice immediately, authorize the motion to dismiss as primary strategy, and keep the settlement path -- with its carrier consent and special committee requirements -- as a contingency only if the motion to dismiss fails.
